newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian coffee sector sees red over buoyant peso.
newsitem.headline: Colombian coffee sector sees red over buoyant peso.

text.p: Colombia's coffee industry has lost $2.8 billion over the past six years because of the peso's steady strengthening against the dollar, Jorge Cardenas, veteran chief of the National Coffee Growers' Federation, said Tuesday.

He spoke in an annual address to the National Coffee Growers' Congress in Bogota where he warned that the industry was being squeezed dry by the peso's surge on the back of Colombia's growing oil income.
"With the (currency's) appreciation the coffee industry is losing all margin for maneuver," Cardenas said.
"Its like being in a hydraulic vice -- inflation raises costs and salaries while appreciation causes income to plummet," he said.

The peso's appreciation, which makes Colombian goods less attractive in the global marketplace, has hit the coffee industry hard because its export revenues have eroded in real peso terms as the domestic currency strengthened.

Among other measures aimed at breathing new life into the sector, Cardenas called for a slash in oil production to curb the amount of petrodollars entering the economy and putting upward pressure on the peso.

He also called for a once-off devaluation of the peso through a change in its daily floating rate exchange band and said a sharp cut in government spending, and external financing of that spending, would help take upward pressure off the peso.

Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo and central bank chief Miguel Urrutia announced Friday that a slight modification of the peso's exchange rate band would allow for a peso devaluation of anywhere between 15 and 29 percent in 1997. But the government had forecast a 13.5 percent devaluation this year and the peso has lost less than 3.0 percent of its value in nominal terms so far.
